patient.name: Unknown Male (approximately 22)
patient.chiefComplaint: Found unresponsive and apneic in a park restroom with drug paraphernalia present

history.hpi: No history is obtainable from anyone on scene. A bystander went to use the single-stall park restroom and found the patient slumped against the wall, motionless and apparently not breathing, and called 911. The entire history must be inferred from the physical exam and the scene: an uncapped syringe and a small piece of burnt foil on the floor beside him, pinpoint non-reactive pupils, faint track marks in the left antecubital fossa, and central cyanosis with apnea. Time of ingestion and substance are unknown.
pastMedical: Unknown; no medical alert jewelry and no information from bystanders
medications: Unknown; scene findings suggest illicit opioid use
history.events: Bystander entered the restroom, found him unresponsive against the wall, and called 911; nobody witnessed the events leading up to it

scene.dispatch: Male subject, unknown age, reported unresponsive near the restrooms at a city park
scene.location: Small, poorly lit single-stall public restroom in a lakefront park; confined working space with a concrete floor
scene.safety: Confined space with an uncapped syringe and burnt foil on the floor. Sharps hazard must be acknowledged and controlled; PPE required and the patient should be moved to a workable space
scene.bystanders: The reporting bystander waits outside and has no information about the patient; no family or friends present
visualCues: Male in his early twenties slumped against the restroom wall, motionless
Marked central cyanosis of the lips and face
Uncapped syringe and a small piece of burnt foil on the floor within arm's reach
Clothing disheveled; left sleeve pushed up above the elbow

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a young male unresponsive to all stimuli including sternal rub, GCS 3, with a flaccid tongue occluding the airway and no respiratory effort whatsoever. A carotid pulse is present but slow and weak at 40; no radial pulse is palpable. He is centrally cyanotic with a saturation of 68 percent. Pupils are pinpoint and non-reactive, and there are faint track marks in the left antecubital fossa. This is a respiratory arrest with a perfusing but bradycardic rhythm. The protocol is explicit that airway, breathing, and circulation are supported before naloxone is given, not after.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Flaccid tongue occluding the airway; no gurgling or stridor; opens with a head-tilt chin-lift
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic. No chest rise or fall observed and no air movement felt
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Carotid pulse palpable but slow and weak; no radial pulse; skin cool, clammy, and cyanotic
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Pinpoint at 1 mm bilaterally, fixed and non-reactive to light
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Flaccid; no response to sternal rub or any painful stimulus
otherFindings: Faint track marks in the left antecubital fossa
Uncapped syringe and burnt foil on the floor beside him
No signs of head trauma; no bleeding; no medical alert jewelry
No transdermal patch found on the skin survey

expectedActions.shortAction: Don appropriate PPE and control the sharps hazard before working the patient
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Don the appropriate PPE. Note that opioids have minimal vapor pressure and do not pose an exposure risk to rescuers unless aerosolized or ingested. Be aware that unsecured hypodermic needles may be on scene if the intravenous route may have been used by the patient, and that there is a higher risk of needle sticks during the management of this patient population which may also have an increased incidence of blood-borne pathogens.
expectedActions.rationale: The uncapped syringe on the floor of a cramped restroom is the realistic hazard here. The protocol also settles the myth that ambient fentanyl exposure endangers rescuers.

expectedActions.shortAction: Open the airway, insert an OPA, and BVM ventilate at 1 breath every 6 seconds
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For apnea, provide one breath every 6 seconds adjusting based on pulse oximetry and digital capnometry or capnography (with the goal of 35-45 mmHg).
expectedActions.rationale: He is apneic with a saturation of 68 percent. Effective ventilation is the life-saving intervention and it is what fixes the bradycardia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Ventilate before medicating: support ABCs before giving naloxone
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Critical resuscitation (opening and/or maintaining the airway, provision of oxygen, ensuring adequate circulation) should be performed prior to naloxone administration.
expectedActions.rationale: This is the sequencing decision the scenario is built around. Naloxone takes minutes to work; the hypoxia kills in that window if nobody is ventilating.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose to rule out hypoglycemia as the cause of the altered mental status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess the patient for other etiologies of altered mental status including hypoxia (pulse oximetry less than 94%), hypoglycemia, hypotension, and traumatic head injury.
expectedActions.rationale: Scene findings suggest opioids but do not prove them. The protocol requires the other reversible causes be excluded rather than assumed away.

expectedActions.shortAction: Naloxone 2 mg IN (adult 0.4 to 2 mg IV/IM, up to 4 mg IN), titrated to respiratory effort
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Adults: The typical initial adult dose ranges between Naloxone 0.4-2 mg IV, IM, up to a dose of 4 mg IN or 5 mg ETT. The administration of the initial dose or subsequent doses can be incrementally titrated until respiratory depression is reversed.
expectedActions.rationale: The protocol dose is a titrated range with a stated endpoint of adequate respiratory effort, not a fixed maximal dose given all at once.

expectedActions.shortAction: Keep ventilating while the naloxone works; use the lowest effective dose
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Regardless of the doses of naloxone administered, airway management with provision of adequate oxygenation and ventilation is the primary goal in patients with confirmed or suspected opioid overdose. Opioid withdrawal: Patients with altered mental status secondary to an opioid overdose may become agitated or violent following naloxone administration due to opioid withdrawal therefore the goal is to use the lowest dose as possible to avoid precipitating withdrawal.
expectedActions.rationale: Ventilation does not stop when the drug goes in. Over-dosing naloxone buys a combative patient and a lost airway rather than a better outcome.

expectedActions.shortAction: Survey the skin for a transdermal opioid patch and remove any found
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Legally prescribed opioids are also manufactured as an adhesive patch for transdermal absorption, and if found, should be removed from the skin.
expectedActions.rationale: A patch left in place keeps dosing the patient long after the naloxone has worn off.

transitions.condition: Crew opens the airway, places an adjunct, and begins effective BVM ventilation with high-flow oxygen before administering titrated naloxone, continuing ventilation while the drug takes effect. Within two to four minutes he takes a sudden deep gasping breath, resumes spontaneous respirations, and opens his eyes, agitated and confused.

Crew delays ventilation to prepare and give naloxone first, or fails to establish an adequate airway and effective ventilations. Over two to three minutes the hypoxia and bradycardia worsen until the carotid pulse is lost and the patient arrests in a non-shockable rhythm.

phases.name: Ventilated first; naloxone given
phases.description: Two to four minutes after the naloxone the patient takes a sudden deep gasping breath, then resumes spontaneous adequate respirations. His color improves to pink and warm, his heart rate rises to 88, and his blood pressure normalizes. He opens his eyes and is immediately agitated and confused, pulling at the oxygen mask and trying to stand up. He is in acute withdrawal, and the crew now has a scene-safety and persuasion problem on top of a medical one: the reversal is temporary and he is going to want to leave.
phases.triggerCondition: Effective BVM ventilation was established before naloxone was given and continued while the drug took effect. Spontaneous respirations have returned and the patient is awake but agitated from precipitated withdrawal.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent and self-maintained; adjunct removed as his gag returned
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Spontaneous at 16 per minute with adequate tidal volume
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse now palpable, strong and regular; skin pink and warm
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities purposefully; pushing crew hands away and trying to sit up
otherFindings: Agitated, confused, and disoriented to place and time
Pulling at the oxygen mask and the monitor leads
Diaphoretic with piloerection and yawning consistent with acute withdrawal
Stating he is fine and wants to leave
No focal neurologic deficit; no evidence of head injury
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Where am I? What did you do to me? Get off me, I'm fine, I'm not going to any hospital."

expectedActions.shortAction: Stay ready to manage the airway again after the reversal
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: EMS clinicians should be prepared to initiate airway management before, during, and after naloxone administration and to provide appropriate airway support until the patient has adequate respiratory effort.
expectedActions.rationale: The BVM does not get packed away because he woke up. He can re-sedate at any point during transport.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish rapport and use verbal reassurance to calm him before anything else
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish patient rapport: Attempt verbal reassurance and calm patient prior to use of pharmacologic and/or physical management devices.
expectedActions.rationale: Withdrawal agitation is expected and predictable. The protocol puts verbal de-escalation ahead of chemical or physical management, and it is what keeps this scene safe.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Agitated or Violent Patient/Behavioral Emergency

expectedActions.shortAction: Explain that naloxone wears off within an hour while the opioid lasts four or more
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Clinical duration of naloxone: The clinical opioid reversal effect of naloxone is limited and may end within an hour whereas opioids often have a duration of 4 hours or longer. Monitor the patient for recurrent respiratory depression and decreased mental status.
expectedActions.rationale: This specific fact is the argument for transport. He needs to hear that he can stop breathing again after the crew leaves, and it needs to be documented that he was told.

expectedActions.shortAction: Prepare a repeat naloxone dose and continued airway support if he re-sedates
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: High-potency opioids may require higher and/or more frequently administered doses of naloxone to reverse respiratory depression and/or to maintain adequate respirations.
expectedActions.rationale: Illicit fentanyl analogs commonly outlast a single naloxone dose, so the second dose is drawn up before it is needed.

transitions.condition: The crew de-escalates verbally rather than escalating, keeps airway equipment at hand, and clearly explains the recurrent respiratory depression risk. He calms, accepts monitoring, and agrees to transport.

phases.name: Transport accepted after counseling
phases.description: The patient has calmed and agreed to transport after the crew explained that the naloxone will wear off well before the opioid does. He remains awake with adequate spontaneous respirations, monitored continuously with the BVM and a second naloxone dose at hand. All interventions are complete and no further change in presentation is expected.
phases.triggerCondition: Verbal de-escalation succeeded, the recurrent-respiratory-depression counseling was given and documented, and the patient consented to transport with continued airway readiness.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse strong and regular; skin pink, warm, and dry
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities normally; cooperative on the stretcher
otherFindings: Oriented to person, place, and event; still irritable but cooperative
Continuous waveform capnography and pulse oximetry in place
BVM and a second naloxone dose staged at the head of the stretcher
Counseling on recurrent respiratory depression documented
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Alright. If you say I could stop breathing again, I'll go. I just didn't want to wake up like that."

phases.name: Ventilation delayed; arrest
phases.description: Two to three minutes were spent preparing and giving naloxone while the patient stayed apneic, or the ventilations delivered were ineffective. The hypoxia and bradycardia have progressed and the carotid pulse is now lost. Organized electrical activity remains on the monitor with no pulse and no obtainable pressure: this is PEA arrest from untreated respiratory arrest. The crew must move immediately to compressions and the cardiac arrest algorithm, and must not spend any more time on naloxone.
phases.triggerCondition: Ventilation was delayed or ineffective while naloxone was prioritized. Progressive hypoxia and bradycardia have deteriorated into pulseless electrical activity.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Requires an adjunct and manual maintenance; no protective reflexes
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No carotid or femoral pulse; blood pressure not obtainable; organized narrow complexes on the monitor
otherFindings: Pulse check confirms pulselessness with organized electrical activity
Mottling appearing over the knees and shoulders
Low EtCO2 consistent with the arrest state
Hypoxia identified as the reversible cause

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm pulselessness and start high-quality chest compressions immediately
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: The most important therapies for patients suffering from cardiac arrest are prompt cardiac defibrillation for shockable rhythms and minimally interrupted effective chest compressions. Initiate chest compressions in cases with no bystander chest compressions or take over compressions from bystanders while a second rescuer is setting up the AED or defibrillator.
expectedActions.rationale: The rhythm is organized but there is no pulse. Compressions start the moment the pulse check is complete.

expectedActions.shortAction: Do not delay compressions for naloxone: it has no benefit in cardiac arrest
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Naloxone has no benefit in the treatment of cardiac arrest. Do not delay other interventions such as chest compressions and ventilations.
expectedActions.rationale: The instinct at this point is another dose of naloxone. The protocol closes that door explicitly.

expectedActions.shortAction: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO early in the first or second round for this non-shockable rhythm
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If feasible, IV or IO access should be obtained. Administer Epinephrine 1mg during the first or second round of compressions. Prioritize early administration of epinephrine for non-shockable rhythms.
expectedActions.rationale: PEA is non-shockable, so the protocol moves epinephrine up rather than waiting through rhythm checks.

expectedActions.shortAction: Ventilate at 10 per minute without interrupting compressions; treat hypoxia as the cause
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: BVM ventilation at 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 10 compressions), applied during the upstroke between compressions, without interrupting the compressions.
expectedActions.rationale: This arrest is hypoxic in origin, so oxygenation and ventilation carry more weight here than in a primary cardiac arrest, but still must not interrupt compressions.
